explanation: Fires on tokens inside legal/court-opinion boilerplate: case captions, procedural phrases and rule citations (e.g. the space before a rule number in 'Rule 73(a)', 'Tex. R. App. P. 8.2', 'This matter [is] before the court', 'pro [se]', 'Defendants [and] Appellants', 'motion for [partial] summary judgment'). Context (being in a court document's header or procedural text) matters more than the token; legal-ish words in news text fire only weakly.

Fires mid-word or mid-compound in technical/scientific jargon: subword continuations of long scientific terms ('struct-urally', 'evolution-arily', 'metabol-ically', 'leuc-ine'), positions inside chemical names (commas in '1,2-diols', isotope brackets '[3H]', '99mTc'), and hyphenated compound modifiers ('multi-purpose', 'full and authentic'). Strongest in chemistry/biomedical abstracts; ordinary prose barely fires.

Mixture. Strongest and most consistent case is '#define' right after an '#ifndef X_H' include guard in C/C++ headers; it also fires on 'No.' starting the docket line after a case caption ('..., Respondent.\nNo.'), 'Category:' in wiki footers, and assorted early subword tokens in names or foreign words ('I-bb-i-Sin', 'P-ero-xisome', Finnish/Hungarian words). It responds to a token that starts a predictable structural line following a header.

Fires on 'that' right after a noun (or verb) that takes a content clause or relative clause: 'evidence that', 'a message that', 'a theory that', 'a proposal that', 'recommend that'. Strongest when the preceding word is a noun like evidence/idea/message/info/theory/statement; weaker for plain relative 'that' after ordinary nouns, and near zero for other function words.

No clear shared theme: fires on completions of fixed or stock phrases across very different registers, e.g. 'com[edy]' in 'fantasy-comedy film', 'P[.S].', '(AP [Photo]', 'Getty Images[/B]BC', 'guess [what]', 'such a thing [as]', 'do not [edit] by hand', code keywords ('end loop', 'package', 'Promise'). Roughly a 'highly predictable next piece of a set phrase' detector, but too diffuse to predict reliably.

Fires in promotional/descriptive prose about places, companies or publications, on the token right after the named entity or in a 'one of the / a ... ' description: 'Denver['s] top hotels', 'one of [the] most tempting', 'Las Vegas is truly [a] city', 'The Finnish [tech] titan', 'India['s] largest IT firms'. Also fires on the verb 'turn/turned' (turn to a professional, turn right, turned to). So two jobs: describing a place/organization's reputation, and 'turn'.

Weak, heterogeneous unit (top examples are near 50% except the max). Fires on subword completions of technical/medical/proper-noun words ('radios[urgery]', 'DB[S]', 'radi[ol]abeled', 'DiCap[rio]', 'nivolum[ab]', 'methad[one]'), on 'cosmic [microwave]', and on "require[('../]" in JavaScript. Mostly predictable continuations of specialized terms, but several unrelated pieces.

Fires on structured/boilerplate tokens in code and machine-formatted text: the final seconds digit in timestamps ('17:34:3[3]'), doc-comment tags ('@version'), 'All rights [reserved]', class/type names after 'class' or 'implements', 'using System[;]', HTML tags like '<li>'. Common theme is code or metadata headers rather than prose; prose tokens give almost nothing.

Fires on outcome/benefit words in evaluative text about results or performance, especially medical outcome and marketing benefit language: 'reporting [excellent] long-term results', 'driving [significant] savings', 'short[-term] results', '30[-day] complication rate', 'poor [clinical] outcomes', 'with [good] result', '[improve]', '[better] insights'. The token is the adjective/verb describing how good the outcome is.

Fires in formal technical/patent/scientific exposition on the function word or period that closes a predicate: 'relates [to]', 'binds [to]', 'accounts [for]', 'reveal [the]', and on sentence-ending periods in background statements of patents or abstracts ('...clean technologies[.] An important aspect'). Patent 'The invention relates to' is the clearest case; casual text and code fire weakly.

Hard to characterize: fires on mid-phrase tokens in fixed formula-like sequences across contexts, e.g. license boilerplate ('LICENSE [file]', 'file [that] was distributed', 'Use [of] this source code'), stack traces ('line 77,[ in]'), 'et [al].', 'MEMORANDUM AND [ORDER]', numbers ('12 [million]'). Loosely 'continuation of a stock phrase', but it's a mixture.

Mixture: fires on '<script' tags in HTML, Go 'errors.New', subword endings of medical terms ('sten[osis]', 'tampon[ade]', 'R[hythm]', 'melanocort[in]', 'blood [gas]'), and blank lines after wiki/web section headers ('Club career

', 'About

'). No single shared concept.

No coherent pattern: fires on assorted tokens such as 'dollar [sign]', 'whitelist [these] domains', 'Acad[emia]', a math variable '$[a]$', 'Firefox', a comma in 'JANUARY 1, 200x', 'prior [written] permission' in license text, 'Published [online]', 'README[.md]'. Cannot predict reliably beyond some preference for boilerplate and technical text.

Mixture: fires on zeros inside long runs of zeros ('0000[0]0000'), 'This [file] is part of' in source-code license headers, and various mid-word subword pieces (Hungarian/Turkish suffixes, 'rein[vest]', 'best[ow]', 'proof-of-con[cept]'). The 'This file' header and zero runs are the most predictable parts.

Fires on the second digit of a two-digit number beginning with '2' (e.g. the '4' in '24', '2' in '22', '8' in '28'), especially for ages, hours ('24 hours'), days of the month and times. Other leading digits (1x) or digits inside years and long numbers give moderate or weak activation.

Fires on tokens inside award/honor titles and achievement or evaluation phrases: 'Player [of] the Year', 'Excellence [in]', 'Award for [Excellence]', 'most valuable [player]', 'a measure of [success]', 'efficiency [evaluation]', 'Most Influ[ential]'. Also a smaller offshoot on 'possession' in criminal charges. Main job is awards/excellence/success assessment.

Fires on inner subword pieces of long anatomical/medical (mostly Greek/Latin-derived) words, e.g. 'oes[ophage]al', 'lary[nge]al', 'acet[ab]ular', 'cere[bell]ar', 'Spl[en]omegaly', 'macro[ceph]aly', 'peric[ard]ial'. The word being split into subwords and being anatomical matters; whole-word tokens and non-medical text barely fire.

Fires on nouns naming the shape of measured data in science: 'distribution', 'curve(s)', 'spectrum/spectra', 'peak', 'maxima', 'decay functions', especially after a qualifier like 'Maxwell-Boltzmann', 'normal', 'recovery', 'FTIR'. Related words about shape/peak (shape of, peaked, broadened) fire moderately.

Fires on the token that starts an identifier or label component right after a separator: the space before a number ('No. 3', 'ID 1', '= 4'), the hyphen or underscore in compound codes ('HLA-A24', 'Na,K-ATPase', 'L-arginine', 'ui_320'), and the initial letter after a delimiter ('No. A047'). Roughly 'beginning of an alphanumeric code/ID part'; occasional coordinating 'and' fires too.

Fires on the auxiliary/copula verb that starts a question after subject-auxiliary inversion: 'what [am] I doing wrong', 'or [is] it', 'and [have] we lost', 'Why [can] I', '[Has] anyone', 'will I'. Requires the question context (wh-word, 'or', sentence start of a question); declarative auxiliaries fire weakly.

Fires on the first subword fragment of a word split into pieces, especially proper names or foreign words ('[Gr]ays', 'Wax[h]aw', '[Mir]amar', 'Bolsonaro, que [p]one', 'P[UBLISHED]', 'muss [gesch]rieben'). The token is an incomplete word start whose continuation is not yet determined; full words and code barely fire.
